Module 4: Genomic Selection

Optional self-study

Use BIGapp to estimate predictive ability with cross-validation and generate genomic predictions.
Author

Alexander M. Sandercock

Published

December 14, 2025

Modified

July 13, 2026

Workshop path

  1. Overview
  2. Setup

Lesson at a glance

  • Time: optional self-study, about 30 minutes plus computation
  • Start with: local BIGapp, the filtered VCF, and phenotype CSV
  • Do: distinguish model evaluation from generation of predictions
  • Save: validation results, predictions, settings, and sample definitions

Genomic selection uses markers across the genome to predict genetic merit. In BIGapp, we have two related tasks:

  • Predictive Ability uses repeated cross-validation to evaluate out-of-sample prediction within the available phenotyped data.
  • Genomic Prediction fits a model and returns predicted phenotypes and estimated breeding values, or EBVs.

This module is optional because both analyses can take longer than the guided two-hour session.

Why Use Genome-Wide Prediction?

Phenotyping can be slow, seasonal, expensive, or destructive. Wouldn’t it be useful if we could use marker information to help decide which candidates should advance to those costly stages?

That is the basic idea. We combine observed phenotypes with marker relationships in a training set, then estimate values for genotyped candidates. Genomic prediction does not eliminate field evaluation. It gives us another source of evidence for deciding what to test next.

Unlike a GWAS, this workflow is not trying to interpret one significant locus at a time. Many markers can jointly contribute information, including through their relationship to unobserved trait loci.

Training and Prediction

The training data contain both genotypes and observed phenotypes. A fitted model can then predict samples that have genotypes but no phenotype for the selected trait.

Figure: Escamilla et al. (2025), open-access article, licensed CC BY-NC-ND.

Prediction depends on trait architecture, phenotype quality, genotyping, model, relatedness between training and target samples, and validation design. There is no universal predictive-ability rating or minimum training-population size that applies to every breeding decision.

Before we fit a model, we need to define the trait, candidate set, and intended use. We also need to decide what current selection process the model should be compared with. Those choices determine which validation design is useful.

Part 1: Predictive Ability

BIGapp repeats cross-validation and reports the correlation between predicted and observed values for each iteration. Before treating that correlation as evidence for a breeding decision, read Cross-validation accuracy for genomic prediction.

Cross-validation separates model fitting from evaluation. We hold out some records, predict them without using their phenotypes for training, and compare the predictions with the observations. Repeating that split shows us how sensitive the result is to a particular fold assignment.

The important part is not just the number of folds. The held-out samples should mimic the prediction problem we actually care about as closely as the available data allow.

Figure: K-fold cross validation, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

  1. Select Predictive Ability under Genomic Selection.
  2. Under Choose VCF File, upload the filtered VCF from Module 1.
  3. Under Choose Trait File, upload atlantic_giant_pumpkin_diversity_phenotypes.csv.
  4. In Trait File Options, select NA and Sample_ID, review the preview, and select Save.
  5. Set Species Ploidy to 2.
  6. Set Iterations to 5 for a short demonstration.
  7. Under Select Trait(s), choose Fruit_Weight_lbs.
  8. Leave fixed effects and Advanced Options (beta) unchanged for the core exercise.
  9. Select Run Analysis.
  10. Review Violin Plot, Box Plot, and P.A. Table. Save the table with the settings used.
TipPredictive Ability answer

The table contains one result per iteration, and the plots summarize that distribution. Values can change between runs because fold assignment is random. Record the full distribution, the iteration count, the method and relationship matrix, and the samples included. Do not reduce the exercise to a fixed expected correlation.

Part 2: Genomic Prediction

  1. Select Genomic Prediction under Genomic Selection.
  2. Upload the same filtered VCF and phenotype CSV.
  3. In Trait File Options, select NA and Sample_ID, then save.
  4. Set Species Ploidy to 2.
  5. Under Select Trait, choose Fruit_Weight_lbs.
  6. Leave fixed effects and Advanced Options (beta) unchanged for the core exercise.
  7. Select Run Analysis, review the confirmation, and proceed.
  8. Inspect Predicted Pheno Table and EBVs Table.
  9. Use Save Files to retain the output and analysis settings.

The default single-VCF workflow fits with samples that have trait records and returns results for samples in that VCF. Advanced Options (beta) can accept a separate prediction VCF and alternative method or relationship-matrix settings. Use advanced settings only when the training and target marker sets, allele coding, sample IDs, and ploidy have been checked.

Interpreting the Output

An EBV is a model-based estimate for a defined trait and target population. A candidate ranking is useful only if the validation represents how we plan to use the model.

Random folds can look better than the real prediction problem when close relatives occur in both the training and test folds, or when future predictions will target a different cycle, environment, or population.

The predicted-phenotype table uses the trait scale supplied to the model. The EBV table contains the model’s estimate of genetic merit under the selected settings. Before interpreting either table, check the sample IDs, missing phenotypes, and direction of selection for the trait.

TipGenomic Prediction answer

The output should contain a Predicted Pheno Table and an EBVs Table for Fruit_Weight_lbs. Numerical values depend on the fitted data and selected settings. Compare rankings only within the saved run, and do not treat the simulated regional pattern as a recommendation for selection.

Discussion Questions

  1. What future samples or breeding cycle should the validation mimic?
  2. Could relatives occur in both training and test folds?
  3. Which fixed effects would be known at prediction time?
  4. How would you compare genomic prediction with the program’s current selection process?
  5. What information must be saved so another analyst can reproduce the ranking?

Next Steps

  • Review Cross-validation accuracy for genomic prediction.
  • Read the in-app parameter and results help before using advanced options.
  • Report software issues through the BIGapp issue tracker.

Key Takeaways

  • Predictive Ability evaluates out-of-sample prediction within a validation design.
  • Genomic Prediction fits a model and creates predicted-phenotype and EBV outputs.
  • Validation must resemble the samples and decisions for which the model will be used.
  • Save the folds or iteration settings, model choices, input identities, and complete output distribution.

Finish: Review the dataset guide, or return to the workshop overview.
